override.title: Is your Function Chart still right?
override.headline: Is your Function Chart still right?
override.support: In Metronome: open Function Chart. Test it against how last quarter went.

panels.heading: No owner?
panels.support: Name the person who will own it.

notes: At a quarterly, put the current Function Chart on the screen. Ask where ownership was unclear last quarter, then fix the chart.
Restate the rule: every function has one accountable owner. One person is accountable for the work. Others may be responsible to contribute to the work.
In private mode, each person writes who holds each function; reveal, then agree. Resolve differences about current accountability. Add any new or planned functions.
Finish when every function has one owner who said yes out loud.
Allow about 25 minutes, with the Team View after it.
Open the Team View in Metronome on the screen. Fix any difference from the chart now.
When one person owns two functions, it shows in red: a load to watch. Planned functions show where people can grow.
Each owner says their critical number out loud. It answers one question: did I have a good day? A person who owns two functions names one for each.
Show the Team View to the whole team at a town hall whenever it changes.
The critical number can be financial or not. A good place to start is what the function hands to the next one.
override.title: Check your Team View and critical numbers.
override.headline: Check your Team View and critical numbers.
body: Every function and its owner is in the Team View.
Each owner says their critical number: the one number that tells them whether they had a good day.
override.support: In Metronome: open Team View. Check it against your Function Chart.

override.title: Are your scorecards complete?
override.headline: Are your scorecards complete?
override.support: In Metronome: open Scorecards. Each leader answers in turn.
body: Is your own scorecard complete?
Does each of your direct reports have one?
If not, name the date.
notes: At a quarterly, this is a check-in. The homework was for every leader to complete their function scorecard in Metronome.
By this session, each leader's direct reports have a scorecard too. Each leader rates their direct reports against it on the A-Player grid. If any are missing, say so now and agree a date.

A scorecard is one page for a function. It says what success looks like: a purpose in one sentence, three to five functional accountabilities, each starting Owns, exactly two metrics, six to eight key competencies, and the company's Core Values. The two metrics are one widget the owner controls and one fiscal metric the role owns.
The company's Core Values go on every scorecard. If the team has agreed them, check they are there. If not, they go on once the team agrees them.
Scorecards are reviewed every 90 days. The scores: 0 below, 1 meets, 2 exceeds. The owner scores first, then their team lead, then they talk about the differences.
Homework: complete the annual reviews on the function scorecards in Metronome.

override.support: In Metronome: open KFFM. Put it on the screen.
notes: If the KFFM is not in Metronome yet, use the example drawing on the next slide.
Each owner colors their own function by where its critical number stands against target: on track is green, at risk is yellow, needs attention is red. Red is a conversation, not a verdict.
body: The 3 to 5 key functions are still the right ones.
Each owner rates their function red, yellow or green, by its critical number.
What will it take to turn it green?

override.title: For each lever: did you push it? What moved?
override.headline: For each lever: did you push it? What moved?
notes: At a quarterly, the six levers are the check on the KFFM. The KFFM is only right if the team is using it to move more cash faster.

Open the team's own KFFM in Metronome beside this drawing. Go lever by lever. For each one, ask its owner what they did to push it last quarter and what moved. A lever nobody is pushing is a finding. Write it down.
Quantity and conversion: every hand-off has a named widget. Each widget is countable, and it is not revenue or cash. Its owner controls it and counts it every week.
Price: has a good Profit per X emerged? If not, leave it blank.
Timing: add the days each function really took last quarter. Where did the work wait? Which function added the most days? Compare with the days the team estimated last time.
Capacity is how many widgets a function can handle in a month. A function can be fast and still too small.
Cost: what each function costs to run.
Each critical number should tell the owner whether the function is working. Focus on a few, at most four, on the KFFM.

override.title: Pick one lever, then review the KFFM every week.
override.headline: Pick one lever, then review the KFFM every week.
override.support: In Metronome: open KFFM. Which lever moves cash fastest?
body: Make that lever a candidate for a QHAG priority.
Add the KFFM to the weekly leadership meeting.
Every week, each owner reports their critical number: red, yellow or green.
A red number needs a written plan: situation, cause, correction, follow-up.
notes: The team picks the lever that moves cash fastest this quarter. Take it into the QHAG as a priority candidate.
New at this session: the KFFM joins the weekly leadership meeting. That is where the team watches the lever it picked.
The weekly meeting reviews the numbers on the KFFM in Metronome. It does not redraw the KFFM. The KFFM changes at the quarterly.
Homework: review the KFFM in every weekly leadership meeting.

override.title: Test each Core Value.
override.headline: Test each Core Value.
override.support: Is it a value you hire and fire on, or a brand value?
notes: A value that fails the tests is a brand value or a wish, not a Core Value.
A fourth or fifth value can earn its place here.
Allow about 10 minutes.
body: When did you last let someone go for not living it?
Does someone who keeps breaking it belong here?
Would you build a new company around it, in any industry?
Then ask: is an important value missing?

override.support: In Metronome: open One Page Plans. Read your Core Purpose aloud. What needs to change?

override.headline: Does your BHAG still hold?
override.title: Does your BHAG still hold?
override.support: In Metronome: open One Page Plans. Read your BHAG aloud.

override.title: Is your Market Map still right? Are your top competitors on it?
override.headline: Is your Market Map still right? Are your top competitors on it?
notes: Put the team’s own Market Map on the screen. The example here is a reminder of its parts.
Ask what changed in the market last quarter. Check that the top competitors are on the map. The team scores them next.
Homework: update the Market Map in the War Room in Metronome.

override.title: Is your Core Customer still right? Read their needs aloud.
override.headline: Is your Core Customer still right? Read their needs aloud.
notes: Put the team’s own Core Customer on the screen. The example here is a reminder of its parts.
Read the three ranked needs aloud. The team tests the white space against them next.
Change only what is no longer true.
Homework: update the Core Customer in the War Room in Metronome.
Ask a leader to read the 3HAG aloud. Invite the team to identify contradictions and untested assumptions.
Test it against the 3HAG line: does each capability build an attribute where the company will lead?
Question the math: do the widget targets add up to the revenue?
Change only what fails or is no longer true. Anything unresolved goes on the homework list with an owner.
This is the purpose of the day. Give the first test the most time: does each capability build an attribute where the company will lead?
override.support: In Metronome: open One Page Plans. Read your 3HAG aloud. Then test it against your 3HAG line.
body: Each capability builds an attribute where you will lead.
The statement and the “known for” describe the future company.
The numbers are set: date, revenue, cash and widgets.
Every number has an owner, and the widgets support the revenue.
Decide: what in the 3HAG changes?

notes: Read the 1HAG aloud, top to bottom, then run the six checks.
The status review already showed where the 1HAG stands. Test it against the 3HAG line the team drew.
Change only what fails or is no longer true. Anything that fails goes on the homework list with an owner.
override.support: In Metronome: open Annual Priorities. Read your 1HAG aloud. Then test it against your 3HAG line.

notes: Every leader independently lists what must be accomplished this quarter to deliver a 1HAG priority, then shares.
At a quarterly, the candidates include last quarter’s open priorities, the lever picked on the KFFM, and what the white space changed.

Run the six questions from the “Pick the priorities that contribute most to success” slide on each candidate. Hover over “six questions” to show them. In a 90-day window, “How soon will we see it?” counts for more.
The team ranks the survivors together. At least 80 percent agreement supports 100 percent commitment.
Challenge vague aspirations and repeated revenue targets. Ask which specific work will produce the result.
Invite debate and explore disagreement. Do not let the CEO answer for everyone. Ask holdouts what the team may have missed; seek full commitment after discussion.
Ask an owner to claim the #1 priority aloud. Check they have the capacity and skills; preferably not the CEO.
Agree on the done-by date, the measure of success and the date it will be achieved by.
Done is not the same as success. The owner commits to the done-by date. The achieved-by date is when the number must have moved. If it has not moved by then, find out why and fix the cause.
override.support: What must you get done now to deliver the 1HAG?
body: List candidates: last quarter’s open priorities, your 1HAG priorities, the lever you picked and what the white space changed.
Test each with the six questions, then rank.
Agree on the owner, done-by date, measure of success and achieved-by date.

override.support: In Metronome: open Quarterly Priorities. Read your QHAG aloud before you move on.

notes: Start with the widgets, then take the priorities in rank order. The owner of each lane drafts it and the team questions it.
Building the plan together develops the team as much as the plan.
Allow about 45 minutes.
Homework: add each lane’s steps as sub-priorities under its company priority in Metronome.
Widgets: a weekly number shows a miss while there is time to act. Ask each owner: can you reach this week’s number? The weekly numbers add up to the quarter’s targets.
Lanes: the team sees each week how the priority gets done. Lanes belong to company priorities, never to a function. Each lane keeps its priority’s owner.

Steps: a step can be a decision made, a test run, a result verified or a checkpoint. It only has to be real and checkable. A live priority that cannot name its weekly work is too vague, or too small for a lane.
If the answer is no, change the plan now. Move a step, change an owner or drop a priority.
Lanes show the work. They are not the measure of success. That stays on the QHAG.
The weekly leadership meeting reviews sprint lane status.

override.headline: How are your meetings going?
override.title: How are your meetings going?
override.support: In Metronome: open Meetings. For each: running? Working? What to change? Rate it 0, 1 or 2.

panels.heading: Daily huddle
panels.support: 7 to 10 minutes, every day except the day of the weekly meeting.
items: Metrics: yesterday’s widget actual and today’s forecast
The #1 thing to get done today
Stucks, and anything that can’t wait

panels.heading: Weekly 1:1
panels.support: 15 to 30 minutes. Each leader with each direct report, led by the direct report.

panels.heading: Weekly leadership meeting
panels.support: 60 minutes or less. The CEO owns it.

notes: Give it about 10 minutes, on the board’s Meeting Rhythm Check-In.
Rate each meeting: 0 below, 1 meets, 2 exceeds expectations.
All five meetings should be running: the three here, the Monthly Town Hall and Quarterly Planning.
New today: the KFFM review joins the weekly leadership meeting.
The daily huddle’s facilitator rotates.
The scoreboard shows last week’s widget forecast, the actual and this week’s forecast.

override.title: Is your Monthly Town Hall working?
override.headline: Is your Monthly Town Hall working?
override.support: In Metronome: open Meetings. Running? Working? What to change? Rate it 0, 1 or 2.
notes: Rate the Town Hall the same way as the other meetings: 0 below, 1 meets, 2 exceeds.
It runs 30 to 45 minutes, with everyone. The CEO owns it.
Values recognition: name someone in front of the whole company. Name the value. Name what they did.
This is the only meeting where the whole company hears the same thing at the same time.
Financial transparency builds the financial literacy of the whole team.
Show the Team View at a Town Hall only when it changes.

override.support: Write them together now. Each leader shares them with their team tomorrow.
